stories.title: Waymo Borrows Its Way Into the Global Taxi Business
stories.story:
For most of its existence, Waymo has been an equity story — a moonshot funded by Alphabet's deep pockets and a succession of venture rounds that lifted its valuation to $126 billion earlier this year. Yesterday, something structurally different happened. Waymo closed its first-ever private debt deal, and lenders wanted more of it than the company had originally planned to sell. What started as a target of roughly $3 billion was upsized to $5 billion, with PIMCO, Blackstone, and Sixth Street Partners among those buying in, arranged by Goldman Sachs and priced at 5.25 percentage points above the benchmark rate.

The shift from equity to debt is not cosmetic. Equity investors absorb losses if the company fails; debt investors get paid first, which means Waymo is now accountable to a harder clock. The loan is unrated — no credit agency has blessed it — so lenders did their own underwriting of a company burning cash to chase a target of one million paid rides per week across twenty cities worldwide by year's end. It currently runs roughly 500,000 weekly rides across fourteen to fifteen U.S. markets. International launches in London, Tokyo, and Munich are in the pipeline.

The mechanism driving the capital need is straightforward: AI inference costs and fleet procurement scale faster than revenue when you are doubling city-by-city simultaneously. Debt lets Waymo grow without further diluting equity, but it introduces a repayment obligation that equity never had. The deeper implication is competitive: private credit flowing into robotaxis at this scale signals that institutional finance now treats driverless transport as infrastructure — like a toll road or a data center — rather than a research bet. When the money categorizes you differently, the world tends to follow.
stories.hook: The moment a moonshot starts borrowing like a utility company, it's no longer a moonshot.

stories.title: Google Buys a Nuclear Reactor's Worth of Power Without Building One
stories.story:
The oldest question in the AI arms race is not which model wins — it is who controls the electrons. Google answered it this week with a deal that is clever precisely because it avoids the hardest problem in energy: building something new.

On October 6, Google signed two interlocking agreements with Constellation Energy, the largest nuclear operator in the United States. The first is a 20-year power purchase agreement for 890 megawatts of nuclear power — roughly the output of a brand-new reactor — extracted not from a new reactor but from upgrades to 11 aging ones across Illinois, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey. Modernizing turbines, steam generators, and control systems at plants already licensed and running is orders of magnitude faster and cheaper than breaking new ground. The first upgraded megawatts are expected to flow by 2028. The second agreement locks in an additional 2,700 megawatts from Constellation's broader fleet over 15 years, giving Google a total of 3.59 gigawatts of contracted power — enough to light more than 600,000 homes — flowing through the PJM Interconnection, the grid serving 67 million Americans.

Constellation's stock jumped 12 percent on the news. The deal unlocks $4.3 billion in Constellation investment and sustains roughly 4,400 existing union jobs while creating 7,200 construction positions. But the structural story is larger than any one company. Amazon struck a similar deal with Constellation just last week. Microsoft is backing the Three Mile Island restart. The pattern is unmistakable: Big Tech is quietly privatizing the financing of America's aging nuclear fleet, trading long-term revenue certainty to operators in exchange for guaranteed baseload power. Evercore estimates that economically justified reactor uprates could add four to eight gigawatts of additional nuclear power by the mid-2030s.

The implication cuts two ways. AI data centers are getting their power. But the public grid — and every ordinary ratepayer on PJM — is also, for once, getting new baseload supply rather than losing it to corporate off-takes.
stories.hook: The fastest way to build a new nuclear reactor in 2026 is apparently to let Google pay someone to upgrade an old one.
stories.source: CNBC / Reuters / Constellation Energy press release, October 6, 2026

stories.title: China's AI Labs Are Raising Billions Before Anyone Can Stop Them
stories.story:
DeepSeek has blown past its own fundraising target. The Hangzhou-based AI lab set out to raise roughly $7.4 billion ahead of a planned 2027 IPO on Shanghai's STAR market. Investor demand — turbocharged by the release of DeepSeek's V4 Flash model, which outcompetes OpenAI and Anthropic on cost and performance benchmarks — pushed the round toward $12 billion, with term sheets suggesting it could approach $15 billion. Tencent and CATL, the battery giant, are among the largest backers.

Meanwhile, Beijing-based Moonshot AI quietly closed its final private round at a $50 billion valuation — up from $31.5 billion just this summer — and is targeting a Hong Kong IPO in Q1 2027 that could raise up to $5 billion. Its annual recurring revenue is on track to double to $2 billion by December. The two companies together are absorbing more private capital in weeks than most national AI programs spend in years.

Here is the complication that gives the story its edge: Chinese regulators have opened a data-security investigation into both DeepSeek and Moonshot. The probe adds a structural wrinkle that matters to any foreign investor reading an IPO prospectus — state oversight in China can delay listings, restrain business models, or simply transfer leverage to the government at the moment of greatest company value. The race is between the labs' need to lock in capital before IPO windows close, and Beijing's parallel interest in asserting control before these firms become too autonomous to manage. The money is moving fast. The regulators are watching.
stories.hook: The most interesting thing about China's AI fundraising boom isn't the numbers — it's that the government opened investigations into both companies the same week they started investor roadshows.

stories.title: SAP Buys the Map of Your Workforce Before AI Redraws It
stories.story:
The anxiety driving corporate boardrooms right now is not whether AI will eliminate jobs — it is whether anyone inside those organizations actually knows what skills their people have before the restructuring begins. SAP's agreement to acquire TechWolf, a Belgian AI company, announced October 6, is a direct bet that the answer is almost always no.

TechWolf's core product is a 'context graph for work' — a continuously updated model built by ingesting a company's existing HR and business systems, then mapping three things: the granular tasks inside each job, the skills individual employees actually apply, and how that compares to the external labor market. That sounds like HR software jargon, but the mechanism is consequential. Most large enterprises have personnel records that describe job titles, not capabilities. When a wave of automation hits a department, leadership has no reliable way to know which people could be redeployed to higher-value work and which face a genuine skills gap. TechWolf is the instrument for that diagnosis.

SAP will embed TechWolf into SuccessFactors, its human-capital management suite used by thousands of companies globally — giving TechWolf instant scale that would have taken years to build independently. The practical implication: workforce-restructuring decisions that today rely on manager intuition or blunt surveys will increasingly be made by a model with continuous, evidence-based visibility into what the organization can actually do.

The deeper story is that this acquisition reveals where the real AI-era business value is accumulating: not in the models that automate tasks, but in the systems that tell organizations what to do with the people left behind.
stories.hook: The bottleneck in every AI restructuring isn't the technology — it's that no one knows what their people can actually do.

stories.title: Private Equity Buys the Hospital Drip, Moves It Home
stories.story:
On October 6, drug distributor McKesson and private equity firm Clayton Dubilier & Rice agreed to take Option Care Health private in a $5.8 billion deal, paying $32.05 per share — a 37% premium to where the stock had been sitting in the low $20s all summer. Option Care is the largest independent home and alternate-site infusion services company in America, treating more than 308,000 patients a year across 197 locations for conditions that once required hospital admission: rare diseases, orphan-drug therapies, complex chronic conditions.

The structure is deliberately layered. CD&R takes 51%, McKesson puts in $1.4 billion for 49%, and a pre-wired clause lets McKesson buy out CD&R's stake later — making this less a joint venture than a staged acquisition with a private equity chaperone. Five banks, including Goldman Sachs and Barclays, are providing committed financing. Option Care canceled its earnings call the morning the deal was announced and withdrew its 2026 guidance entirely.

The logic runs deeper than dealmaking opportunism. Hospital systems are expensive, understaffed, and politically unpopular. Payers have spent a decade pushing complex therapies out of inpatient settings. McKesson, already a dominant drug distributor, gains a national delivery platform for the specialty and rare-disease drugs it already moves through the supply chain — closing the loop from manufacturer to patient's living room. For CD&R, it is a familiar playbook: buy a sector leader in a structurally growing market, use leverage and operational focus to expand margins, then sell or float when multiples recover.

The risk is antitrust. The deal needs Hart-Scott-Rodino clearance, state-level healthcare approvals, and a shareholder vote. Arbitrage traders see the spread: the stock closed roughly $1 below the deal price, implying a closing timeline stretching into mid-2027 at best.
stories.hook: When the hospital is too expensive, private equity builds a hospital that comes to you.
